Female Mosshead sculpin (Clinocottus globiceps) attain sexual maturity at a total length of approximately 6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 6 centimeters], a size that corresponds well with values reported for the congeneric species Clinocottus analis. This threshold marks the onset of vitellogenesis and the ability to participate in spawning events, which in the rocky intertidal zone generally occur during the cooler months of the year. Newly hatched individuals emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs and carry a substantial yolk sac, weighing only about 0.0023 grams [Wwb = about 0.0023 grams] at the moment of eclosion. This minuscule birth mass is characteristic of cottid fishes and reflects an initial reliance on endogenous yolk reserves prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. The transition to active feeding typically coincides with the complete absorption of the yolk sac and the opening of the mouth gape, a critical developmental window that determines early survival in the variable splash-pool environment this species inhabits.

In a series of captive rearing trials conducted at a stable water temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C], the maximum annual reproductive output of Clinocottus globiceps was assessed through direct observation of spawning females. Based on extrapolation from the closely related Clinocottus analis, each female deposits roughly 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = roughly 1 to 3 eggs per clutch], with approximately one clutch produced daily [F_R_i = approximately one clutch produced daily] during the peak of the breeding season under these controlled thermal conditions. This high-frequency, low-fecundity strategy is unusual among sculpins and may represent an adaptation to the unpredictable availability of suitable nest sites in the high intertidal zone. It remains unclear whether warmer or cooler temperatures would substantially alter this pattern of gamete release and successive spawning events.

The ultimate total length attained by a fully grown Mosshead sculpin reaches 19 centimeters [Li = 19 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger-bodied members of the intertidal sculpin guild along the northeastern Pacific coast. This maximum recorded length is reached only after several years of growth, during which the fish show a pronounced allometric shift in body depth and fin ray ossification. The corresponding ultimate wet body mass for an individual of this length has been estimated at 134 grams [Wwi = 134 grams], derived from a length-weight regression fitted to a sample of field-collected adults. This considerable adult mass, which is over fifty thousand times the mass at hatching, underscores the dramatic ontogenetic increase in tissue accumulation that occurs between the lecithotrophic larval phase and the robust, nest-guarding adult stage. Such a growth trajectory is consistent with a life history that delays reproduction until a relatively large body size is achieved.

Longevity records for Clinocottus globiceps, again inferred from studies of Clinocottus analis maintained under similar thermal regimes, indicate that the species can attain a maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years] when reared at 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C]. This is a notably long lifespan for a small-bodied intertidal fish and may reflect the low metabolic costs associated with a cool-water existence and a relatively sedentary, benthic lifestyle. The oldest documented individuals are typically those that have successfully navigated the high mortality risks of the pelagic larval phase and the intense competition for crevice shelters among adults. By the time senescence occurs, these fish have usually completed multiple reproductive cycles, contributing eggs to several successive breeding seasons. The 8-year (8 years) [am = 8 years] maximum lifespan represents a physiological limit that appears to be linked to the gradual deterioration of organ function under stable, cool temperatures at a temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C].

Comparative analysis with other cottids reveals that the Mosshead sculpin's life-history strategy is shaped by its occupation of a highly dynamic thermal habitat. While the maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years] and the female size at puberty of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters] align closely with values for Clinocottus analis, the ultimate length of 19 centimeters [Li = 19 centimeters] appears to be slightly greater than typical for that congener, possibly reflecting differences in local prey availability or intertidal at a temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C] pool productivity. The remarkably small hatchling mass of 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams] is consistent with the small egg diameters characteristic of sculpins that produce multiple clutches per season. In contrast, the adult wet weight of 134 grams [Wwi = 134 grams] represents a substantial investment in somatic tissue that likely contributes to the species' ability to defend territories and withstand periodic wave exposure. These collectively paint a portrait of a species that matures at a modest size, lives a relatively long life, and invests in repeated, low-fecundity spawning events.
